title: What the House Remembers
subtitle: Tuesday 17 to Thursday 19 October 1893: The Old Woman on Ferry Lane, the Crypt in the Rain, the County Clerk's Libers, the Closed Wing by Day

setting.name: Haverkill, the crypt, Poughkeepsie and the north wing by daylight, nights 3 to 5
setting.description: Three days of history and three nights of the house. By day the party is free until sunset: down the hill to Haverkill, where the church, the newspaper, the undertaker and the oldest woman in the village each hold part of 1852; out to the Greywick crypt at the end of the orchard in Wednesday's rain; down the river line to the Dutchess County Clerk's office in Poughkeepsie, where the deed that made the fortune is copied into Liber 97; and into the closed north wing, where nothing can happen in daylight and everything already has. By night the household tightens: a séance in the drawing room on Tuesday, a young man with a supper tray on the north stair on Wednesday, Conrad and his hired men at the dispatch box on Thursday. Every day a new tally mark appears in the river room's doorframe. By Thursday night the party should know the Juffrouw's true name and what was done to her, that her own key opens her door, that Jasper died behind it, and that the key is in Leonora Greywick's workbasket.
setting.atmosphere: Fog on Tuesday, filling the valley to the top of the bluff, so that the house stands on an island in a white sea with the river line trains whistling invisibly underneath. Rain on Wednesday, cold and straight down all day, drumming on the conservatory glass, overflowing the gutters, turning the orchard grass to sponge and the crypt steps to a waterfall. Grey and still on Thursday, with the leaves down and the Catskills gone. The village is kind and nosy; Poughkeepsie is brisk and indifferent; the past is in ledgers, on stones and in an old woman's memory, and it is all quite clear once someone bothers to read it. In the house the gas seems dimmer every night. Linus's voice behind the north door is weaker. Count the marks.

keyLocations.name: Gerrit Brouwer's Cottage
keyLocations.description: A stone cottage by the walled kitchen garden, with a vine on the porch, a stove, two dogs, a rack of fishing rods, a lever-action rifle over the door and an iron poker driven upright into the doorframe of his own bedroom, which he has never taken out. Gerrit came down from Columbia County in 1855 to dig the foundations of the new house, stayed, and remembers it being built round the stone house.
features: The poker in the doorframe: driven into the jamb so the bedroom door cannot swing shut
Gerrit's pipe rack and his clay pipe, and a tin of Dutch tobacco Mrs. Jansen buys him
A photograph of young Mr. Jasper and the outdoor staff in 1870, Gerrit at the end of the row
encounters: Gerrit Brouwer, who will tell the whole of it to anyone who asks him straight, by daylight, away from the house
secrets: CLUE A5, B3, E1 (core for anyone who asks him about 1871, or about the keys): 'October of '71. I'd had a drop, and Mr. Abram was in a temper, and I went in the old kitchen in the stone house to sleep it off where he wouldn't find me, and I shot the bolt. I woke up in the dark, and I was upstairs, in the room at the top. Only it wasn't the room as it is. There was a bed, and a chest, and a fire laid and not lit, and rain on the window, and her, sitting by the window with her back to me. Two nights. I heard Mr. Jasper calling me through the door. Then the second night the door opened, and there was Mr. Jasper with a lamp in one hand and an old iron key in the other, a Dutch key, big as your hand, and his face white as paper. He said, Come out, Gerrit, slow, don't look at her. And I came out. And he drove the poker into the jamb of the stair door so she couldn't shut it on him, and we went down.'

Gerrit will add, with Persuasion DC 12 or a pipe of tobacco: 'Mr. Jasper told me after: only her own key opens her door, and only from outside, and only if you're steady. He tried it on his father's door in '73 and couldn't, because Mr. Abram had the key locked up and Mr. Jasper was abroad. That's what killed the old man. She keeps 'em seven nights. Then she lets 'em go down the stair.' He does not know her name. 'The Juffrouw. That's all anybody ever called her. Old Quell called her that, the steward, and so we all did.'

Gerrit knows the key was on Mr. Jasper's watch chain for twenty years and has wondered where it went. If told that Tuttle's ledger says Mrs. Greywick asked for it, he goes very quiet, and then says, 'She sent me to Poughkeepsie on the twenty-fourth. For seeds. In September.'

keyLocations.name: The Old Stone Church and Its Registers
keyLocations.description: Haverkill's church, built of river stone in 1717 with a steep roof and a wooden bell-cote, a gallery, box pews and a pulpit with a sounding board; the churchyard slopes down toward the river with three centuries of Haverkill under it. The consistory room behind the pulpit holds the registers in an iron-bound chest: baptisms, marriages and burials since 1717, and the consistory's minute books, in Dutch until 1790 and English after. The Reverend Cornelis Vreeland has been dominie here for nineteen years and buried Jasper Greywick on 4 October.
features: The register chest and the minute books, which the Reverend will open for anyone who asks politely
The churchyard: Roelofs graves along the north wall back to 1720, with a gap after Hendrick Roelofs, 1847; and down by the gate, a plain stone: 'Jotham Quell, died 17 October 1853, aged 44'

A marble tablet on the church wall, put up by subscription of the river men in 1853: 'To the memory of Captain Sabina Roelofs of the sloop Zwaluw, of this congregation, lost upon the river, October 1852. They that go down to the sea in ships.'
encounters: The Reverend Cornelis Vreeland, kind, scholarly, curious, and Leonora Greywick's pastor
secrets: CLUE D2 (core for anyone who reads the registers with the Reverend; Research DC 12 to find it quickly): Sabina Roelofs, baptised 3 June 1821, daughter of Hendrick and Neeltje Roelofs; admitted a member 1839; and in the consistory minute of Sunday 10 October 1852: 'Miss Roelofs absent from the Lord's Table. Mr. Abram Greywick reports that she has gone to New York upon business.' The minute was written on the seventh night of her keeping, the night she died.

The river men's tablet (a second version of CLUE D1) gives her name and the word 'Captain'. The Reverend says the old men used to stand in front of it on the anniversary and say her name aloud, 'a river custom, for the drowned, so they know they are remembered'. That custom stopped thirty years ago. (Points toward Rule 4.)

Jotham Quell's stone: died 17 October 1853. Research DC 13 in the burial register: 'Jotham Quell, steward at Greywick, found dead in the house after a week's illness.' The same words, almost, as Abram's in 1873.

Vreeland knows Leonora as a devout and generous parishioner. Insight DC 14: he is troubled by something she said to him after the funeral, which he will repeat if the party gives him a reason: 'She asked me whether a sin that God has not been told about can be punished in this world. I said I thought it was usually the other way round.'

keyLocations.name: Ferry Lane: Mrs. Annetje Vedder
keyLocations.description: A two-room clapboard cottage at the bottom of Ferry Lane, a hundred yards from the old stone pier, with geraniums in the window, a Dutch Bible on the table and a stove kept red-hot. Mrs. Annetje Vedder is eighty-eight, nearly blind, sharp as a tack, and the oldest person in Haverkill. In 1852 she was forty-seven, the wife of Pieter Vedder who sailed mate on the sloop Zwaluw, and housemaid to Captain Sabina Roelofs in the stone house on the bluff.
features: A daguerreotype in a little leather case on the mantel: a woman of about thirty in a dark dress and a man's pea jacket, square-faced, level-eyed, her hair pulled back, one hand resting on a ship's wheel
Pieter Vedder's sea chest under the window, and in it the Zwaluw's pennant
Coffee, which she makes very strong, and a dish of olykoeks for visitors
encounters: Mrs. Annetje Vedder, who has waited forty-one years for someone to ask her
secrets: CLUE D4, F4 (core for anyone who asks about the stone house, the Roelofs or 1852): 'Juffrouw Bina. Sabina Roelofs. Captain of the Zwaluw, like her father, and better at it. I kept her house. On the Monday, the fourth of October, Mr. Abram came up and sent me home with a month's wages, and said the Juffrouw was going down to New York on the night boat Tuesday. She never went. I know she never went, because her trunk was still in her room, I saw it through the window from the path, and she never in her life went anywhere without her trunk and her glass. And she never went to New York on business, because she did her business in Poughkeepsie, at the courts. They said she drowned. She could swim the river at the Landing and back. I said it, then. Nobody listened to a sloopman's wife.'

CLUE B4 (core): 'When the Juffrouw was home, there was a lamp in the river window, for the boatmen. A lit window meant the captain was home and resting, and you could come up to the house with your business in the morning. When she was away, it was dark. After she went, it was dark for years, and then somebody started lighting it again. I thought, well, somebody up there knows.'

CLUE H2 and the anchor (core): 'She signed everything with her name and a little anchor after it, like this,' (she draws it on the table with a wet finger) 'her father did the same. She never wanted a penny that was not hers. She wanted what was hers, and the Landing kept for the sloops and the farmers, and Mr. Abram wanted it for his railroad.' The daguerreotype: anyone who has seen the Juffrouw (DC 15 fear check, and they know her at once). Annetje will lend it to someone she trusts.

If Dory Oudekerk is with the party, Annetje touches her face with both hands and says, 'You're Marritje's. You have her face, the Juffrouw's face. Did your grandmother keep the letter?' (Ties to CLUES D5, F2.)

keyLocations.name: The Haverkill Advertiser and Phineas Tuttle's Parlour
keyLocations.description: Two doors apart on Main Street. The Advertiser's office: a flatbed press, cases of type, a smell of ink and paraffin, the bound files of every issue since 1838 on shelves to the ceiling, and Mr. Silvanus Lemmon, the editor, who will let anyone read them for a dime and a story. Tuttle's: a parlour with plush chairs and a ticking clock, a showroom of coffins, a back room the public does not see, and the ledgers, in which Phineas Tuttle writes down everything about every funeral he has ever conducted, because his father did.
features: The Advertiser's bound files: October 1852, October 1853, October 1873
Tuttle's ledger for 1893, a tall book bound in black leather, with an entry for every body and every effect
Tuttle's showroom, where a party member may be measured for a coffin by a man who is only being polite
encounters: Silvanus Lemmon, editor, who smells a story
Phineas Tuttle, undertaker, solemn, precise, and fond of Mr. Jasper
secrets: CLUE F3 (core for anyone who reads October 1852): Saturday 16 October: 'It is feared that Miss Sabina Roelofs of this village, owner of the Landing, was lost overboard from the night boat on the night of the 5th inst., she not having arrived in New York. Mr. A. Greywick, her partner, is prostrated.' Saturday 23 October, at the foot of a column of river news: 'The agents of the Night Line state that no passenger of the name of Roelofs was booked on any of their boats in the first week of this month.' Nobody followed it up.

CLUE A6 (core for anyone who reads October 1853 or 1873): 22 October 1853: 'Jotham Quell, steward at Greywick, was found dead on Monday at the foot of a stair in that house, after a week's seclusion through illness.' 25 October 1873: 'The Hon. Abram Greywick died at Greywick on Saturday, of apoplexy, having been shut up in his study a full week.' Lemmon, if asked: 'The old men always said the stone house got them. River talk.'

CLUE E3 and G2 (core for anyone who reads Tuttle's 1893 ledger, or asks him what Jasper wore): 'Oct. 1. J. A. Greywick, Esq. Received from the house 9 a.m. Rigor complete; dead some hours. Nails of both hands broken and torn; splinters of dark wood under them, removed. Effects: gold hunter watch (Tiffany), chain, carnelian seal, one small old iron key. Oct. 3: key removed from chain and returned to Mrs. G. at her request, as a keepsake. Watch, chain and seal to be buried with deceased by her wish.' Tuttle remembers the splinters: 'Old oak. Very old, dark, hard. Not from any door in that new house.'
Tuttle is a friend of Dr. Wyle and will open his back room and his ledger for the doctor without any check at all.

keyLocations.name: The Greywick Crypt
keyLocations.description: A granite mausoleum at the far end of the orchard, on the lip of the bluff, with a bronze door green with weather, two steps down into a vaulted chamber lined with shelves of coffins, and a lower vault beneath reached by an iron ladder. Gerrit keeps the key; there is a second on the strongroom board. It is a quarter of an hour's walk from the house through the orchard, longer in rain.
features: Abram Greywick's coffin, with a silver plate: 'Abram Greywick, 1806 to 1873. He made the river serve.'
Jasper's coffin, newest, on the lowest shelf, with fresh lilies gone brown
A white marble tablet on the back wall, put up by Jasper in 1874, with no grave beneath it: 'Sabina Roelofs, partner in the Line, lost from the night boat October 1852. Forgive us.'
The lower vault, where the rain comes in through a cracked drain, the water stands an inch deep, and the rats live
encounters: A Rat Swarm in the lower vault, roused by lamplight and noise; it pours up the ladder if anyone goes down (use the Rat Swarm entry; it flees from fire and from open daylight at the door)
The clock: the light goes at about 5:15, and every person named in the will must be under the roof by then
secrets: CLUE D1 (core): the tablet, with her full name, and its last two words.

CLUE G3 (core for anyone who opens Jasper's coffin; Dr. Wyle, or Medicine DC 12, to read it): the body of a man who starved and went thirsty for a week; under the nails of both hands, where Tuttle missed a few, splinters of black oak; on the watch chain, a small bright ring where something has been taken off it. Opening a coffin without the widow's consent is a crime and a sin, and the GM should make it feel like both. Honora, as his daughter, may give her own consent and bear it. Fear check DC 20 for the truth of it, for anyone who looks properly; the GM describes no more than a thin face, folded hands and the broken nails.
If anyone matches the splinters to the river room's door (gw-scenario-002, the closed wing), Investigation DC 12 makes it certain: the same 1734 oak, dark as iron, the same grain.
Nothing supernatural happens in the crypt. Sabina's rules are the house's, and this is not the house. Let the rain and the dead and the clock do the work.

keyLocations.name: The Dutchess County Clerk's Office, Poughkeepsie
keyLocations.description: Twenty-five minutes down the river line, a walk up from the station to the courthouse on Market Street. The County Clerk's office is a long high room of iron-railed shelves holding the libers of recorded deeds and mortgages since 1718, with grantor and grantee indexes, a counter, a deputy clerk, and a sign saying that searching is ten cents a liber. The steamboat company's agent has an office on the waterfront below.
features: The grantor index under R: Roelofs, Sabina, to Greywick, Abram, Liber 97 of Deeds, page 212
Liber 97, page 212: a clerk's fair copy of the deed, with the original signature traced in facsimile, as the clerks of 1852 did for disputed hands
The steamboat agent's old purser's books, in a back room, which the agent will let anyone see for a dollar
encounters: Mr. Wilbur Fosdick, deputy clerk, who has never been asked about anything older than 1880 and is delighted
secrets: CLUE D3, F1 (core for anyone who searches the index; Research DC 13 to do it in an hour, otherwise it takes the afternoon and the party must run for the 4:12): 'Sabina Roelofs, spinster, of Haverkill, to Abram Greywick of the same, for one dollar and other good and valuable consideration, the Landing at Haverkill with the pier, wharves, warehouse and the stone dwelling house, and four hundred acres of the bluff. Dated 4 October 1852. Acknowledged the same day before Elkanah Brush, Commissioner of Deeds. Recorded 8 October 1852 at two o'clock p.m.' The traced signature reads 'S. Roelofs', in a fine hand, without an anchor. Elkanah Brush, Fosdick finds in the index, was Abram Greywick's own clerk.

Insight or Research DC 12, comparing with anything Sabina signed (Annetje's memory, Dory's letter, the logbook in the north wing): every true signature has a small anchor drawn after the name. This one does not. It was recorded on the fifth day of her keeping, while she was locked in the river room.
The steamboat agent's purser's book for the Night Line, October 1852: no Roelofs on any boat in the first two weeks. (Corroborates CLUE F3.)

Fosdick, for Research DC 14: no letters of administration were ever granted on Sabina Roelofs' estate. She was never proved dead. Under the law, her heirs could have claimed the Landing at any time; nobody told them they could.

keyLocations.name: The North Wing by Day
keyLocations.description: The stone house of 1734, entered by daylight with Mrs. Quell's key or Gerrit's, or the strongroom board's. Nothing happens here between sunrise and sunset; the GM should say so, plainly, the first time the players go in, once they have earned it by asking. The cellar kitchen: low, vaulted, whitewashed long ago, with a hearth eight feet wide and a great hearthstone in front of it, and a pantry with a bolt on the inside. The stair: steep, enclosed, dark oak, cold. The river room: the oak door with its 1734 box lock, and inside, an empty room, dusty and very cold, with a sea chest under the window and the lamp on the sill.
features: The doorframe of the river room, inside and out: rows of tally marks scratched into black oak, in sets
The box lock: a Dutch iron lock as big as a Bible, its keyhole the size of a thumb, unpickable with anything the party has, and no other key in the house fits it
The window: small panes, a deep sill with the lamp on it, and letters cut into the sill with a knife long ago
The sea chest: Sabina's, never opened since 1852, with her clothes, her spyglass, and her logbook
The cellar hearthstone: one great slab of bluestone, its mortar a different colour from the rest of the floor
encounters: Mrs. Quell, who will come and find anyone in the north wing within half an hour, and who will not allow anyone to touch the hearthstone
Linus, by day: nothing. The room is empty. Fear check DC 10 for anyone who calls his name and hears nothing at all
secrets: CLUE C5 (core for anyone who looks at the doorframe): the tallies. On the inside of the frame, low down, seven very old marks, fine and straight, made with something thin. On the outside, and inside higher up, other sets: seven, deep and ragged (1853); two (1871); seven (1873); seven, newer, the wood still pale at the bottom of each groove (this autumn). And a last set, fresh, in pale new wood: three on Tuesday, four on Wednesday, five on Thursday. Nobody is in the room. Fear check DC 15.

CLUE D6 (core for anyone who looks at the sill or opens the chest): cut into the sill, small and neat, 'S.R.' and a little anchor. In the chest, her logbook of the sloop Zwaluw, 1847 to 1852, signed on its flyleaf 'Sabina Roelofs, master' with an anchor; its last entry, 2 October 1852: 'Ashore. Letter to M. To Poughkeepsie Monday, by the road, not the boat.'

CLUE E2: the lock. Mechanics DC 20 cannot open it; nothing opens it but its own key. By day the door opens with a push if left unlocked; it is unlocked by day now, Mrs. Quell says, 'it is always unlocked by day'. That is not true at night: when the house is keeping someone, the door is locked from the other side from sunset to sunrise.

CLUE F5 (for anyone who lifts the hearthstone: a crowbar, Athletics DC 14, an hour's work, and Mrs. Quell's furious resistance; fear check DC 20): beneath it, in a shallow grave cut in the clay, wrapped in a sail, the bones of a woman of about thirty, with the back of the skull broken, and in the right hand a hairpin. Dr. Wyle (Medicine DC 12): a fall or a blow against stone; she did not drown. Moving the bones does not lay her. They can be lifted and carried to the churchyard later (gw-scenario-004).

CLUE H3 (anyone with The Thin Place, or anyone who stays in the river room as the sun sets, which is a very bad idea; fear check DC 15): frost forms on the inside of the window, and words are written in it as if by a finger, in Dutch: MIJN NAAM. GEEF TERUG. 'My name. Give back.' Dory, Gerrit, Mrs. Jansen or the Reverend can read it. Then whoever is in the room should leave, at once, before the door closes.

keyLocations.name: Leonora's Sitting Room
keyLocations.description: The warm chintz room on the first floor with the canary, the prie-dieu, the coal fire and the workbasket. Leonora is in it most of the day and all evening; she leaves it for meals, for church on Wednesday morning, for the séance on Tuesday night, and for half an hour after luncheon when she lies down. The maids have been told not to do the grate this week.
features: The grate: a coal fire, and in the ashes at the back, curled black fragments of paper
The workbasket of black silk, full of crape and reels
A locked rosewood writing desk with a brass keyhole
A chatelaine on the dressing table in the bedroom beyond, with scissors, a thimble case, a vinaigrette and, from Wednesday, one more thing
encounters: Leonora, who will come back early from anything if she sees someone on the first-floor corridor
secrets: CLUE G6, B5, E4, H1 (core for anyone who searches the grate; Investigation DC 13 to lift the fragments whole): pages from Jasper's journal, burned on Tuesday night and not quite consumed. Legible pieces in his hand: '...lamp lit, she keeps to her own house, I have seen it forty...' '...only her own key, from outside, and a steady hand. I opened it for Gerrit in ’71 and could not for my father...' '...her name in her room, by our blood, and what we took given back in her hearing. I have not the courage. My children must...' The rest is ash.

CLUE G5 and E (core for anyone who searches the workbasket before Wednesday): under the crape, two keys: a small modern brass key with a tag, 'Blue Room', and an old iron key as long as a finger with a plain round bow. From Wednesday morning only the Blue Room key is there; the iron key is on her chatelaine, which she wears.

The writing desk (Mechanics DC 14): the rest of Jasper's journal, 1858 to 1893, with the last thirty pages cut out. It never names her; it calls her 'the Juffrouw' or 'her'. It is full of the rules as Jasper tested them over forty years. Taking it is theft from a widow, and she will know by evening.

Searching her rooms and being caught means Leonora knows exactly what the party suspects. She does not accuse them. She becomes more careful, and that night she asks Mrs. Quell, in front of everyone, whether the guests have been sleeping well.

synopsis: The party goes looking for the house's history and finds a woman. Gerrit Brouwer tells how he was kept two nights in 1871 and let out by Jasper with an iron key: only her key, from outside, and a steady hand. Mrs. Annetje Vedder on Ferry Lane remembers Captain Sabina Roelofs, the lamp in the river window, the anchor she drew after her name, and the Monday in October 1852 when Abram Greywick sent the maid home and said the captain was taking the night boat. The church register, the river men's tablet and a marble plaque in the Greywick crypt give her name. The Advertiser's files say she was lost from a boat she never boarded, and that the steward and then Abram himself died after a week shut in. In Poughkeepsie, Liber 97 holds the deed to the Landing, dated the night she was locked in, recorded on the fifth day of her keeping, and signed without her anchor by a hand that was not hers. In Wednesday's rain the party opens the crypt, and the doctor finds black oak under Jasper's nails and a bright place on his watch chain where the key was; Tuttle's ledger says Mrs. Greywick asked for it. In the north wing by day, the river room's doorframe is scored with the tallies of everyone she has kept, and a new mark appears every day for Linus. Under the cellar hearthstone, if the party defies Mrs. Quell, lie Sabina's bones. Meanwhile the house tightens: a séance on Tuesday that the dead do not answer the way Leonora hopes, the ghost of a young man with a supper tray on the north stair on Wednesday, and Conrad and two hired guards trying to force Strick's dispatch box on Thursday night. Fanny Ruddock, trusted at last, tells what she saw on 24 September. By Thursday night the party knows the name, the crime, the key and the murderer, and has one night left to save Linus.
hook: Tuesday morning, fog to the top of the bluff, the house an island in a white sea. Gerrit Brouwer is leaning on his rake by the kitchen garden wall when the party comes out, as if he has been waiting. He takes his pipe out of his mouth. 'Mrs. Quell says you're asking about the old wing,' he says. 'Mrs. Quell says I'm to say nothing. Mrs. Quell's a good woman and she's wrong. Come down to my place, where the house can't hear, and I'll tell you how I was shut in up there two nights, and who let me out.'

conclusions.conclusion: D. The Juffrouw is Sabina Roelofs
clues: D1: the tablet in the crypt, and the river men's tablet in the church (the crypt, the Old Stone Church)
D2: the church register and the consistory minute of 10 October 1852 (the Old Stone Church)
D3: the deed in Liber 97 (Poughkeepsie)
D4: Annetje Vedder and her daguerreotype (Ferry Lane)
D6: S.R. and the anchor on the sill, and the Zwaluw's logbook (the north wing)

conclusions.conclusion: F. Abram Greywick took the Landing by forgery while he kept her, and she died in the house
clues: F1: the deed dated 4 October, recorded 8 October, signed without her anchor, acknowledged before Abram's own clerk (Poughkeepsie)
F3: the Advertiser's 'lost from the night boat' and the Night Line's denial (the Advertiser, the steamboat office)
F4: Annetje: the trunk still in the room, the maid sent home (Ferry Lane)
F5: the bones under the hearthstone (the north wing)
D6: her logbook: 'To Poughkeepsie Monday, by the road, not the boat' (the north wing)

conclusions.conclusion: E. Her own key, turned from outside, opens her door (Rule 3)
clues: E1: Gerrit's story of 1871 (his cottage)
E2: the box lock that nothing else opens (the north wing)
E3: Tuttle's ledger: the small old iron key (Tuttle's)
E4: the journal fragment: 'only her own key, from outside, and a steady hand' (Leonora's grate)

conclusions.conclusion: G. Jasper was kept, and Leonora locked him in
clues: G2: Tuttle's ledger: the key returned to Mrs. G. on 3 October (Tuttle's)
G3: oak splinters under Jasper's nails, and the bright place on the chain (the crypt)
G4: Fanny saw Mrs. Greywick lock Mr. Jasper's door on 24 September (Fanny)
G5: the Blue Room key and the iron key in her workbasket (her sitting room)
G6: the burned journal pages in her grate (her sitting room)
G8: Conrad was in New York the whole week (Conrad's telegrams, Cyprian, a wire to the Fifth Avenue Hotel)

acts.title: Tuesday: The Town in the Fog
acts.description: The party goes down into Haverkill, by the drive or the bluff path, and the village opens its memory to whoever asks the right people. Gerrit first, by the garden wall; then the church, the newspaper and the old woman on Ferry Lane, in whatever order the players like. Let the fog close everything in so that each door they knock on is the only thing in the world. Back by sunset; that night Leonora's séance.
objectives: Hear Gerrit's story of 1871 and learn that her own key opens her door
Find Sabina Roelofs' name in the church, the newspaper and Annetje Vedder's memory
Learn about the lamp, the anchor, and what Sabina wanted
Get through the séance, and use it

scenes.name: Where the House Can't Hear
scenes.description: Gerrit's cottage, his stove, his dogs, the poker in his bedroom doorframe. He tells his story (CLUES A5, B3, E1) and answers questions plainly. He is the first person in the campaign to describe the river room as it is at night: the bed, the chest, the fire laid and not lit, the rain on the window that was not raining outside, and her, by the window, with her back to him. He did not see her face. 'You don't want to see her face, I reckon.' He will become the party's companion from here if they want him: he knows the grounds, the crypt, the bluff path and every door in the house.
scenes.readAloud: The old man's cottage is hot as an oven and smells of pipe smoke, dog and apples. He sits on the edge of his bed with his big cracked hands between his knees, and above his head, driven into the frame of his bedroom door so deep that the door can never swing more than halfway shut, is a black iron poker, rusted in place. He sees you looking. 'Forty years,' he says. 'I can't sleep with a door shut. Not since. You want to know what's up there? I'll tell you. It's a room. It's just a room, a lady's room, with a bed and a sea chest and the rain on the window. Only it's raining in there when it isn't raining out here. And it's always night. And she's sitting by the window, with her back to you, waiting. And you can't get out, because the door's locked, and you can hear them, out here, calling you. Two nights I was there. Then Mr. Jasper came.'

skillChecks.success: He tells you the rest (CLUE E1 in full): only her own key, from outside, and a steady hand; Mr. Jasper tried in '73 for his father and could not, because the old man had the key locked away; seven nights, then she lets them go down the stair. And the key was on Mr. Jasper's chain twenty years. He doesn't know where it went. 'Ask the missus. She had the nursing of him.'
skillChecks.failure: He has said what he came to say and will say the rest another day, by daylight, if you come back with tobacco.

skillChecks.success: He is telling the exact truth, and he has told it to no one but Mr. Jasper in twenty-two years. He is afraid of Mrs. Quell's disapproval and more afraid of what will happen to Mr. Linus if nobody does anything.
skillChecks.failure: An old man's story. He believes it, certainly.

skillChecks.success: Kept, not killed: a spirit that holds the living somewhere apart for a fixed term and releases them dead at the end is a spirit repeating what was done to it. Find out what was done to it, and when, and for how long, and you will know its rules. Seven nights is not a number she chose.
skillChecks.failure: A ghost that takes people. You knew that much already.

scenes.name: The Old Woman on Ferry Lane
scenes.description: The heart of the act. Mrs. Annetje Vedder has waited forty-one years for someone to ask. Let her be wonderful: blind, fierce, funny, Dutch-English, insistent on coffee and olykoeks, scornful of the Greywicks and the railroad, tender about the Juffrouw. She gives CLUES D4, F4, B4 and H2, the daguerreotype, and the anchor. If Dory is present, the scene changes: Annetje knows her family face, and the two of them will want to talk alone for a while. The Reverend or the Advertiser can come before or after; the church and the newspaper confirm what she says in ink.
scenes.readAloud: She is tiny, bent nearly double, in a black dress and a white Dutch cap, with milky eyes that look a little to the side of you and hands that find the coffee pot without looking. 'Greywick,' she says, when you tell her where you are staying, and spits, accurately, into the stove. 'Sit. Eat. Nobody comes down Ferry Lane from that house unless they want something, and nobody from that house has wanted anything from Annetje Vedder for forty-one years.' On the mantel behind her, in a little open leather case, a woman in a man's pea jacket looks out of a silver-grey daguerreotype with one hand on a ship's wheel: a square, plain, level face, steady eyes, her hair pulled back hard. 'That's her,' says Annetje, without turning round. 'You've seen her, haven't you. Up there. I can hear it in how you breathe.'

skillChecks.success: She tells it all, from the Zwaluw to the Monday she was sent home, the trunk, the lamp, the anchor, and that the Juffrouw never wanted a penny that wasn't hers, only what was hers. At the end she lends the daguerreotype to whoever she likes best, 'so she can see it, if you get in there. So she knows somebody kept her face.'
skillChecks.failure: She tells you about the Juffrouw, the lamp and the Monday, but she is tired, and offended by something one of you said about the railroad, and she keeps the daguerreotype.

skillChecks.success: There is one more thing she has never said aloud: in the week after the fourth, walking up the bluff path at night to look at the house, she heard someone knocking on the river window from inside, and saw no lamp, and went home and told Pieter, and Pieter said leave it, the Greywicks own the river now. She has never forgiven either of them.
skillChecks.failure: An old woman's grief, sharp as the day it happened.

skillChecks.success: At the Advertiser afterwards, the dates line up: maid sent home Monday 4 October; Abram says she sailed Tuesday 5 October; the paper says lost from the night boat on 16 October; the Night Line says no such passenger on 23 October. And in October 1853, the steward Jotham Quell found dead at the foot of a stair after a week shut up; in October 1873, Abram himself. (CLUES F3, A6.)
skillChecks.failure: The files are vast and the fog has made the office dark; you find the 1852 report but run out of light before the rest. Come back tomorrow.

scenes.name: The Sitting
scenes.description: Tuesday night, nine o'clock, the drawing room, the lamps turned low: Leonora has asked Mrs. Tierney (a player, or an NPC) to hold a sitting, and the household attends, Conrad sneering, Strick disapproving, Mrs. Quell refusing to come and then standing in the doorway. If Aurelia is a player, she runs it, with the GM's help: her tricks (knocks from her shoe, a slate with a hidden message, a ring of salt round the table, which does nothing to the Juffrouw), and then the real thing, which she did not plan. Leonora asks for Jasper: is he at peace, does he forgive. The table answers by going cold, and a slate between two hands writes, in a square plain hand nobody at the table has: MIJN NAAM. Then the gas in the hall goes out. The salt circle was a wrong rite; whoever laid it gains a point of Dread and the Juffrouw knows they tried (that person's bedroom door, that night, swings slowly shut at three, and stops against its iron wedge). While everyone is in the drawing room, Leonora's sitting room is empty, and so is the grate she lit at eight. After the séance she goes up and burns the journal pages; players who are quick and suspicious can catch the smell of burning paper on the first-floor corridor at half past ten.
scenes.readAloud: The drawing room with the gas turned down to blue beads and a single candle on the round table, and the household sitting round it with their hands flat on the cloth, fingers touching, Conrad's hot and damp, the widow's cool and dry. Mrs. Tierney's voice is low and practised and quite beautiful, and for a while there are the knocks you would expect, sharp and obliging, and a sigh from the dark that is very well done. Then the candle flame lies down flat, as if in a wind, though nothing in the room has moved, and the cold comes up through the floor into your feet and your knees and your hands on the table, and the slate that lies between the medium's palms begins to scratch. Nobody is holding the pencil. When the candle stands up again the medium is staring at the slate in her hands as if she has never seen one, and on it, in a square plain hand that nobody at this table writes, are two words in a language only some of you can read.

skillChecks.success: When Leonora asked the dead whether Jasper forgave, she was not grieving: she was afraid of the answer. When the slate wrote, she let out a breath, because it did not say what she feared. She is relieved. Of everyone in the room, she is the only one.
skillChecks.failure: The widow is overcome and has to be helped from the room.

skillChecks.success: MIJN NAAM: 'my name'. Not a message from Jasper. Whoever is in this house wants to be called by her name, and has not been, perhaps for a very long time. And the salt did nothing at all, which tells you something too: this is not the kind of thing salt stops.
skillChecks.failure: Two words in Dutch, and a medium who looks as if she has seen a ghost, which you suppose is her trade.

skillChecks.success: While the household is in the drawing room you slip up to the first floor. Leonora's sitting room is empty, the canary asleep under its cloth, the fire lit; the workbasket is on the table. (CLUE G5: both keys under the crape, the iron one and the Blue Room's.) You are back on the stairs before anyone misses you.
skillChecks.failure: Jem the footman is on the first-floor corridor with coal for the bedrooms and sees you, and tomorrow Leonora knows.

encounters: The séance: a wrong rite (the salt circle) and a true sign (MIJN NAAM); fear check DC 15 for those at the table
Night 3: anyone on the first-floor corridor at half past ten smells burning paper from Leonora's sitting room

acts.title: Wednesday: The Crypt in the Rain
acts.description: Tuttle's ledger in the morning, the crypt in the afternoon, against the clock, in a cold downpour. The point of this act is the murder: the key, the splinters, the bright place on the chain. Opening Jasper's coffin is a crime, an intimacy and a horror, and the players should have to decide to do it. Sunset is 5:14; Gerrit says the walk back through the orchard takes a quarter of an hour in this weather, and the light goes early under rain.
objectives: Read Tuttle's ledger: the torn nails, the splinters, the key returned to Mrs. G.
Open the crypt; find the tablet with her name
Decide whether to open Jasper's coffin, and what it costs
Be back under the roof before sunset

scenes.name: Tuttle's Ledger
scenes.description: Phineas Tuttle, undertaker, a long pale man with a voice like a church organ's lowest stop, was fond of Mr. Jasper and is troubled. He will show the ledger to Dr. Wyle without question and to anyone else for Persuasion DC 12 (Honora, as daughter, automatically). It holds CLUES E3 and G2. Tuttle adds that Mrs. Greywick was very particular that the coffin be closed before the family viewed it, and that she asked for the key herself, on the 3rd, in his parlour, and put it in her reticule. Wednesday morning is also when Leonora begins wearing the iron key on her chatelaine, and when Conrad's telegram brings two hired guards up from Poughkeepsie on the 1:05.
scenes.readAloud: The undertaker turns the great black ledger round on the counter so that you can read it, and runs one long white finger down the column for the first of October, and stops. His hand is very steady. His voice is not. 'I have buried four Greywicks,' he says, 'and my father buried the others. I do not gossip. I write things down.' Under his finger, in a beautiful copperplate: 'Nails of both hands broken and torn; splinters of dark wood under them, removed.' And below, two days later, in the same hand: 'Key removed from chain and returned to Mrs. G. at her request, as a keepsake.'

skillChecks.success: Tuttle gives you the splinters. He kept them, in a folded paper in his desk, because they troubled him: three slivers of wood black as bog oak. 'Not from any door in that new house,' he says. 'That house is walnut and pine. This is old. Very old.'
skillChecks.failure: He shows you the entry and closes the book. 'I have said too much about a client.'

skillChecks.success: Tuttle believes Mrs. Greywick did something wrong, and does not want to believe it, because she is a good churchwoman and paid his bill the same day in cash.
skillChecks.failure: A careful tradesman, protecting his client's privacy.

skillChecks.success: The ledger's next column, the order for the funeral: Mrs. Greywick instructed that the watch, chain and seal be buried with the deceased, but kept the key, and asked for the coffin to be closed and screwed down before the family viewing. A widow who wanted no one to see her husband's hands.
skillChecks.failure: A funeral order: oak coffin, brass handles, lilies, four horses.

scenes.name: The Crypt in the Rain
scenes.description: The set piece. The orchard in a cold downpour, the grass ankle-deep in water, the bronze door, the steps running with rain, the vault inside smelling of wet stone and old lilies, a lantern each. The tablet (CLUE D1) is on the back wall. Jasper's coffin is on the lowest shelf; opening it takes a screwdriver and ten minutes, and Dr. Wyle (or Medicine DC 12) reads the body (CLUE G3). The Rat Swarm is in the lower vault and comes up if anyone goes down the ladder or makes a racket. Run the clock aloud: the light failing, the rain heavier, Gerrit at the door saying, 'It's gone five.' There is nothing supernatural here. The horror is the dead man's hands and the race back to the house.
scenes.readAloud: The rain comes straight down out of a sky the colour of pewter, so hard it bounces off the orchard grass, and the path through the old apple trees is a stream. At the end of it, on the lip of the bluff, with the river invisible in the grey below, the crypt squats under its dripping cornice like something hunched against the weather, its bronze door streaked green. Gerrit's key grates in the lock. Inside it is very dark and very still and smells of wet stone and dead flowers, and the rain is suddenly far away, a hiss beyond the door. The lanterns find shelves, and coffins on them, and silver plates with names: Abram, and Caroline, Jasper's first wife; and on the lowest shelf, newest, under brown lilies, Jasper. On the back wall, white marble glimmers. Someone has carved a name on it, and under the name, two words.

skillChecks.success: (CLUE G3.) A man who starved and thirsted for a week; under the nails of both hands, a few splinters Tuttle missed, black oak, very old; and on the watch chain lying on his waistcoat, a small bright worn ring of gold where something hung for twenty years and was taken off. Fear check DC 20 for anyone who looks properly.
skillChecks.failure: You cannot bring yourself to look closely, or the light is too bad. You see a thin face and folded hands and close the lid again.

skillChecks.success: You read the light and the path and get everyone out and back through the orchard with ten minutes to spare, mud to the knees, soaked to the skin, and the register signed at 5:09 with water dripping onto the page.
skillChecks.failure: The path is a river and someone falls; you reach the terrace door as the light goes. Strick, at the register, looks at his watch and at the window and, being an honest man, rules that the sun had not yet set; but he writes the time, 5:16, and Conrad sees it, and will argue for the rest of the week that someone has forfeited.

skillChecks.success: When the rats come pouring up the ladder from the lower vault, a black squealing tide, you get the hatch slammed down on them with your boot and a coffin-trestle across it, and nobody is bitten.
skillChecks.failure: The swarm is up and into the vault before the hatch closes (Rat Swarm; it scatters from a lantern thrust at it and from the grey light at the door). Fear check DC 10 in the dark.

scenes.name: The Young Man with the Tray
scenes.description: Wednesday night, night 4. A quiet night, and one of the strangest. At midnight, anyone on the first-floor gallery, or anyone keeping watch on the north wing door, sees a young man of eighteen in an old-fashioned coat come along the gallery with a covered supper tray, set it down at the foot of the north wing door, knock twice, wait, and walk away through the wall where the gallery turns; and the tray is gone. He is a Shade: an echo, not a spirit with a will, and he cannot hurt or be hurt (fear check DC 15). It is Jasper Greywick in October 1852, carrying her supper to a locked door for the fourth night. Honora, if played, knows her father's face, young. The Thin Place gives one true impression: shame, and a young man's terror of his father. Let the players talk to him: he does not hear them. If anyone says 'Jasper', he stops, looks round, says 'I'm not to open it. Father says,' and is gone. The same night the new tally appears: four.
scenes.readAloud: The hall clock has just finished striking midnight. Along the dim gallery, from the direction of the main stair, comes a young man walking carefully, the way you walk with something that might spill: a tall thin young man of eighteen or so, in a high-collared coat of a cut your grandfather wore, his hair long over his ears, carrying a tray with a white cloth over it. He does not look at you. He walks to the old oak door at the end of the gallery, stoops, sets the tray down on the floor before it, straightens, and knocks, twice, softly. He waits. His face is pale and his mouth is shut tight, and he is crying without making any sound. Then he turns and walks away along the gallery toward the corner, and at the corner he is not there, and when you look back, neither is the tray.

skillChecks.success: This is a memory the house has kept, not a ghost with a purpose. The young man carried food to that door and knocked and did not open it, night after night, and it has been eating him ever since. If it is Jasper, then Jasper knew all his life exactly what was in that room.
skillChecks.failure: A ghost. A sad one. That is all you can tell.

skillChecks.success: A Shade: the house's echo of something done over and over. It follows no rules of its own and will do the same thing tomorrow night at the same hour. Its presence tells you what the house remembers most: not the death, but the keeping.
skillChecks.failure: You do not know what it was. You know you do not want to see it again.

skillChecks.success: On the tray, before it vanished, under the cloth's edge: a bowl, a cup, a hunk of bread, and a folded paper, which you could not read. On the floor where it stood there is a faint wet ring on the boards, and it smells of river water and tea.
skillChecks.failure: A tray, a cloth, gone.

encounters: A Rat Swarm in the crypt's lower vault (CR 1/4)
The Shade of the young man with the tray on the north gallery at midnight (CR 1/4; it does not fight; fear check DC 15)
Conrad's two hired guards from Poughkeepsie (Night Watchman, CR 1/2, each with a service revolver and a lantern), lodged in the coach house from Wednesday afternoon

acts.title: Thursday: The Deed and the Door
acts.description: Poughkeepsie in the morning, the closed wing in the afternoon, and Fanny's word and Conrad's raid at night. The point of this act is to close the circle: the forged deed proves the crime, the river room proves the keeping, Fanny proves the murder, and Conrad's attempt on the dispatch box shows the players that the living are still acting. By midnight the party should know they must take the key from Leonora before dawn on Saturday.
objectives: Find the deed in Liber 97 and compare the signature
Explore the north wing by day: the tallies, the sill, the chest, the hearthstone
Win Fanny's trust and hear what she saw on 24 September
Deal with Conrad and his hired men at the dispatch box

scenes.name: Liber 97
scenes.description: The 9:15 down to Poughkeepsie, the courthouse, the County Clerk's long room, the indexes and the libers. Wilbur Fosdick, a young deputy clerk with ink to his elbows, is thrilled to be asked about 1852 and helps (CLUES D3, F1). The signature comparison needs something Sabina truly signed: the logbook from the north wing (if they have been there first), Dory's letter, or Annetje's memory of the anchor. The steamboat agent's purser's book is a short walk down the hill. Get them back on the 3:20 or the 4:12 and up the hill by sunset. If a player wants to wire New York about Conrad's whereabouts in September, the Western Union office is by the station (G8: a reply by evening from the Fifth Avenue Hotel confirms Mr. C. Greywick in residence 22 September to 2 October).
scenes.readAloud: Liber 97 is a ledger as long as your arm, bound in red leather gone brown, and when the deputy clerk heaves it onto the counter and opens it at page 212, a breath of old dust and iron-gall ink comes up off the paper. A clerk's fair round hand, forty-one years old: 'This Indenture, made the fourth day of October in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and fifty-two, between Sabina Roelofs, spinster, of the Town of Haverkill...' The Landing. The pier. The stone dwelling house. Four hundred acres of the bluff. For one dollar. At the foot, in careful facsimile, the clerk has traced the signature: 'S. Roelofs'. Nothing after it. And in the margin, in a different ink: 'Recorded 8th October 1852, 2 o'clock p.m.' The fifth day.

skillChecks.success: You find it in an hour, with Fosdick's help, and have time for the rest: the acknowledging officer, Elkanah Brush, Commissioner of Deeds, was Abram Greywick's own clerk (he appears as Greywick's witness on six other deeds); and no administration was ever granted on Sabina Roelofs' estate. She was never proved dead. Her heirs never knew they could claim.
skillChecks.failure: The indexes are a maze; you find the deed by half past three and run for the 4:12 with no time for anything else.

skillChecks.success: Comparing hands: Sabina's true signature (the logbook, the letter) is broad and quick with a little anchor after it. The deed's is narrower, more careful, every letter separately formed, as a man writes when he is copying. A forgery, and not a good one.
skillChecks.failure: The two signatures look different, but forty years and a clerk's tracing could account for that.

skillChecks.success: The steamboat agent lets you see the old purser's books for a dollar, and gossips besides: his predecessor always said the Greywicks paid the Advertiser to bury the Night Line's denial on an inside page. No Roelofs on any boat that October.
skillChecks.failure: The agent is busy and the old books are in a cellar. Come back another day.

scenes.name: The Closed Wing by Day
scenes.description: Into the north wing in daylight, with Gerrit's key or Mrs. Quell's. Say plainly, once, that nothing here can happen while the sun is up. The cellar kitchen and its hearthstone; the stair; the river room door and its tallies (CLUE C5, five fresh marks by Thursday); the box lock (E2); the sill (D6); the sea chest and the logbook (D6). Mrs. Quell arrives within half an hour, and if anyone is near the hearthstone with a crowbar she stands on it. This is her dangerous moment: she will not let them lift it, she will lie ('there is nothing under there but the old well'), she will threaten to tell Mrs. Greywick they have been stealing, and she will, if pushed, take the crowbar and the wing keys away and lock both doors, by day, with nobody behind them. Lifting the stone over her objection (CLUE F5) costs her trust until gw-scenario-003, unless they are kind and show her what they have found. If they show her the deed, Annetje's daguerreotype, or Tuttle's ledger, she sits down on the cellar steps and weeps, and says one thing: 'My father put her there. He told me, the night before he locked his door. I've lit her lamp for twenty-seven years to say I'm sorry.'
scenes.readAloud: The river room is very small, much smaller than you imagined, and colder than the October morning outside: a low ceiling, whitewashed walls gone grey, a floor of wide oak boards silvered with dust, a sea chest under the deep-silled window, and on the sill the brass lamp, cold now, its chimney sooted. Nothing else. It smells of stone, and lamp oil, and very faintly of the river. And the doorframe. Inside, low down, at the height of someone sitting on the floor with their back to the door, are seven short straight marks, fine as if drawn with a pin, so old the wood has gone black in the grooves. Above them, others, in rows, deeper and rougher, made by other hands. And at the end of the last row, in wood still pale and splintery, five fresh marks, the newest one so new you can see the fibres standing up. Yesterday there were four.

skillChecks.success: Reading the frame: seven very old (1852, made with a hairpin, from the floor); seven deep and ragged (1853); two (1871); seven (1873); seven newer, three weeks old, made with fingernails, the grooves stained (this autumn: Jasper); and the fresh five (Linus). Every set but Gerrit's is seven. And the splinters Tuttle gave you match this frame exactly: Jasper's nails were broken on this wood.
skillChecks.failure: Marks in rows, some old, some new. Somebody has been counting something.

skillChecks.success: With Mrs. Quell, on the cellar steps, shown the evidence and spoken to gently: she breaks. Her father, Jotham, told her on 9 October 1853, the night before he bolted his door: 'I helped Mr. Abram with the Juffrouw. She's under the hearth. God forgive me.' She has never told anyone, not even Mr. Jasper, who knew anyway. She will not yet believe it of Mrs. Greywick; she will help with anything else. (CLUE F6, early.)
skillChecks.failure: She takes the keys and the crowbar and locks you out of the wing, and goes to her room, and does not come down to dinner.

skillChecks.success: With the crowbar and an hour's sweat, the hearthstone comes up. (CLUE F5; fear check DC 20.) Under it, in a shallow grave in the yellow clay, wrapped in what was once a sail, she lies, small and brown, the back of the skull broken, a long iron hairpin still in the bones of the right hand.
skillChecks.failure: The stone will not shift, or the bar slips and someone's hand is crushed (1d4 bludgeoning); an hour gone, and the sun lower.

scenes.name: Fanny's Word, and the Dispatch Box
scenes.description: Thursday night, night 5. Two things happen. First, Fanny Ruddock comes to the party, to whoever has been decent to her all week, after the household is abed, and tells them what she saw on Sunday 24 September at about eleven: Mrs. Greywick coming out of Mr. Jasper's bedroom with a candle, turning the key in his door, and putting it in her pocket; and saying, when she saw Fanny on the back stair, 'He walks in his sleep, Fanny. We must keep him safe.' The next morning Mrs. Greywick told the servants he was ill and would see no one, and sent Gerrit to Poughkeepsie for seeds. Fanny has been afraid to say it because she has a secret of her own (her sheet: she has been taking small things from the house and letting the ghost take the blame), and Mrs. Greywick knows it (CLUE G4). Second, at two in the morning, Conrad and his two hired men try to take Strick's dispatch box. Conrad believes, rightly, that the codicil exposes his theft; he means to read it and burn it if it does. The guards come in through the conservatory; Conrad goes to Strick's room, which is not locked, with his revolver. If the party is watching Strick, it is a confrontation in a dark bedroom; if not, Strick wakes and shouts and the house is roused. Conrad will not shoot his own family on purpose, but he is drunk and frightened and the guards are paid to shoot. Whatever happens, Leonora is in her doorway in her wrapper when it ends, watching, and sees exactly where the box is kept and who guards it.
scenes.readAloud: The parlourmaid stands in the doorway with her candle, in her nightgown and a shawl, her hair in a plait, looking about sixteen and very frightened. 'I'll say it once,' she says, 'and then I never said it. The Sunday before Mr. Jasper died. Eleven at night. I was on the back stair with the hot water for Mrs. Greywick's bottle, and she came out of his room with a candle in her hand, and shut the door, and she turned the key in it. From the outside. And she put the key in her pocket. And she looked up and saw me, and she smiled at me, and she said: He walks in his sleep, Fanny. We must keep him safe.' The candle shakes. 'And she knows a thing about me. So I said nothing. And he died.'

skillChecks.success: Fanny is telling the truth, and she is not the only one Leonora has a hold over in this house; she suspects Jem too. She will repeat it to the constable, if someone she trusts stands beside her.
skillChecks.failure: She is frightened; that much is plain. Whether she is right, you cannot be sure from her face alone.

skillChecks.success: In Strick's dark bedroom, with a lantern in Conrad's face: you stare him down. He lowers the revolver, sits on the end of the lawyer's bed and puts his face in his hands. 'Eighty-six thousand dollars,' he says. 'The sinking fund. Father knew. It's in that box, isn't it.' He calls off the guards. (He is a beaten man from here, and a possible ally in gw-scenario-003.)
skillChecks.failure: He fires, wild, in the dark (attack +2 against the nearest, 1d6 piercing), and the guards come running up the back stair with lanterns and revolvers. It is a fight in a bedroom, with an old man and a tin box in the middle of it (two Night Watchmen; use brawling and darkness rules; the guards will stop the moment someone shouts that they are shooting at the family).

skillChecks.success: When it is over, you see Leonora in her doorway along the corridor, in a grey wrapper with her hair down, watching, very still, with one hand closed on the chatelaine at her waist. She has seen where the box is and who sleeps beside it. And on the chatelaine, among the scissors and the vinaigrette, the old iron key.
skillChecks.failure: The household gathers in dressing gowns. The widow is there among them, saying what a dreadful thing.

encounters: Mrs. Quell at the hearthstone: a social obstacle, not a fight; she will physically stand on the stone

Conrad and two hired guards at the dispatch box, 2 a.m. Thursday night (Conrad: Night Watchman stats with a pocket revolver; two Night Watchmen with service revolvers and lanterns); fighting in a dark bedroom (combat.json darkness_and_light)
Night 5: the sixth tally mark appears on Friday morning

npcsInvolved.name: Gerrit Brouwer, 70
npcsInvolved.role: Groundskeeper; the only person ever let out of the river room; companion
npcsInvolved.description: White-bearded, broad, slow, with a hunter's eyes and a clay pipe; a poker driven into his own bedroom doorframe.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To see Mr. Linus out as Mr. Jasper let him out, and the old master's wishes kept.

npcsInvolved.name: Mrs. Annetje Vedder, 88
npcsInvolved.role: The oldest woman in Haverkill; Sabina's housemaid in 1852
npcsInvolved.description: Tiny, bent, nearly blind, in a white Dutch cap; fierce, funny, scornful of the Greywicks, tender about the Juffrouw; keeps her daguerreotype on the mantel.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be believed, at last, before she dies.

npcsInvolved.name: The Rev. Cornelis Vreeland, 53
npcsInvolved.role: Dominie of the Old Stone Church; keeper of the registers; companion
npcsInvolved.description: Lean, stooped, kind, spectacled, a reader of Dutch registers and a whist player; buried Jasper.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To help the living and do right by the dead, and to know what troubled Leonora after the funeral.

npcsInvolved.name: Phineas Tuttle, 50
npcsInvolved.description: Long, pale, organ-voiced, precise; writes everything down because his father did.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To do his duty to the dead, and to be rid of what he wrote on 3 October.

npcsInvolved.name: Silvanus Lemmon, 44
npcsInvolved.description: Inky, eager, sharp-nosed; would sell his press for a real story.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The story. He will print whatever the party gives him, a week late, and the river will read it.

npcsInvolved.name: Wilbur Fosdick, 24
npcsInvolved.description: Thin, ink to the elbows, delighted to be asked about anything before 1880.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To find the deed first, and be thanked.

npcsInvolved.name: Fanny Ruddock, 23
npcsInvolved.description: Sharp, quick, Bowery-born, frightened of Leonora for a reason of her own.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To say what she saw without losing her place or her liberty.

npcsInvolved.name: Mrs. Judith Quell, 61
npcsInvolved.description: Grey, upright, implacable, kind underneath; stands on the hearthstone if anyone comes near it with a crowbar.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep her father's secret buried and the lamp lit. Turns when shown the truth, slowly.

npcsInvolved.name: Leonora Greywick, 52
npcsInvolved.description: Gracious, watchful, always at her workbasket; from Wednesday the iron key hangs on her chatelaine.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To burn the codicil and let the house keep whoever learns too much. She does not yet know how much the party knows.

npcsInvolved.name: Conrad Greywick, 38
npcsInvolved.description: Florid, drinking, sleepless; two hired guards from Poughkeepsie in the coach house from Wednesday.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To read the codicil before anyone else and burn it if it names his theft.

rewards.money: Annetje Vedder will not take money and is offended by it. Silvanus Lemmon pays $10 for the story of the deed, to be printed after Sunday. Conrad, if talked down on Thursday night, gives whoever did it his pocket revolver and a cheque for $100 he cannot cover.
items: Annetje Vedder's daguerreotype of Sabina Roelofs, lent to someone she trusts
The Zwaluw's logbook, signed with the anchor (CLUE D6)
Tuttle's three splinters of black oak in a folded paper (CLUE G3)
A copy of the deed from Liber 97, certified by Fosdick for 50 cents (CLUES D3, F1)
The scorched journal fragments (CLUES B5, E4, H1, G6)
The Blue Room key (CLUE G5), if taken from the workbasket
Gerrit Brouwer's poker, offered to anyone who needs to hold a door

twists: The players will want to take the iron key from Leonora as soon as they know she has it. Let them try. Before Wednesday it is in her workbasket and can be stolen (Sleight of Hand DC 14 while she is out); from Wednesday it is on her chatelaine, and taking it means a confrontation or a very good pickpocket (Sleight of Hand DC 18). If they get it early, she knows, and she changes her plan: she will try to get it back, and on Friday she will try to make the house keep whoever has it.

Mrs. Quell is the obstacle of this scenario, and she is not a villain. She will lie, stand on the hearthstone, lock the wing and threaten to tell Mrs. Greywick about the party's searching. All of it is to protect her dead father's name. Shown the truth with kindness, she becomes the party's strongest ally in the house.

Conrad's raid on Thursday night is a red herring the players can see coming. It proves he is desperate and armed; it does not make him the murderer. Talked down, he gives up his New York alibi without being asked (CLUE G8), and becomes a frightened, useful man for Friday.
If a player is the medium, the séance is hers to run, and the slate's MIJN NAAM is the first thing in her career she did not do herself. Give her the moment. Then give her the Dread.

If the party lifts the hearthstone, Sabina's bones are evidence of murder and the beginning of her burial, not her laying. Moving them changes nothing in her rules. The Reverend will bury them in the Roelofs row, under her own name, when the party is ready (gw-scenario-004).
dmTips: This is the investigation scenario. Budget an hour and a half for Tuesday, an hour and a half for Wednesday, and an hour and a half for Thursday. Most players will not visit everything; the three-clue structure means they do not need to.

Keep the sunset clock in view every day. Name the time when they leave the house and when they reach each place, and remind them of the 4:12. The will's condition is the campaign's isolation: they can leave by day, but not by night.
Annetje Vedder is the emotional centre of the history. Play her with relish. She is the first person who calls the Juffrouw by her name and loves her.
The crypt is pure atmosphere and the hardest moral choice so far. Do not force the coffin open; let the players decide. If nobody will, Tuttle's ledger and the tallies carry the same truth.
Count the tally marks aloud each day: three on Tuesday, four on Wednesday, five on Thursday, six on Friday morning. Say: 'Seven is the last.'
The Young Man with the Tray is the campaign's quietest scene. Resist making him dangerous. He is the house remembering that Jasper knew.

Fear checks: the tallies (DC 15), the slate (DC 15), the daguerreotype for anyone who has seen her (DC 15), the bones and Jasper's hands (DC 20). Rites tried this scenario that are wrong: the salt circle, holy water in the river room, prayers at the door. Each costs a point of Dread, and the Juffrouw notices: that night the person's door swings shut at three against its wedge.
End on Thursday night with Leonora in her doorway, the iron key on her chatelaine, and the party knowing it. Linus has one night left.
